title: Building Projects Taught Me More Than Just Writing Code
excerpt: The past few months have taught me something I did not fully understand when I first started learning how to code. Building a project and learning how to code are not...
body:
The past few months have taught me something I did not fully understand when I first started learning how to code.

Building a project and learning how to code are not always the same thing.

When I was starting, I thought progress meant learning more programming languages, frameworks, and tools. I wanted to understand React, Next.js, databases, AI, APIs, and everything else that seemed important.

Those things are important.

But building projects taught me lessons that tutorials could not.

Tutorials Show You the Path

Tutorials are useful because someone has already figured out the difficult parts.

You follow the steps. You write the code. Something appears on your screen.

At the end, you have a working project.

The problem is that building something from a tutorial does not always teach you what happens when there are no more instructions.

That is where building your own projects becomes different.

You have to decide what to build. You have to think about how different features connect. You have to fix problems that no tutorial mentioned.

Sometimes you spend hours trying to solve something that eventually turns out to be a small mistake.

That can be frustrating.

It can also teach you more than finishing ten tutorials.

Projects Create Problems You Did Not Expect

When you build your own idea, the work becomes less predictable.

A feature that sounds simple can suddenly affect several parts of the application.

A database structure might need to change. An API might return unexpected data. A design that looked good in your head might not work once you actually use it.

You start realizing that development is not only about writing code that works.

It is also about making decisions.

You learn how to break large problems into smaller ones. You learn when to search for answers and when to experiment. You learn that rewriting something is sometimes better than continuing to fix it.

Those lessons are difficult to get from simply following instructions.

Finishing Matters More Than Starting

I have started many ideas that sounded exciting at the beginning.

The first few hours are usually the easiest part.

You have the idea. You imagine what the finished product could look like. You start designing and writing code.

Then the less exciting part arrives.

You find bugs. Features take longer than expected. Some ideas do not work.

That is usually where many projects stop.

Finishing a project, even a small one, teaches something important. A product does not become useful because the idea was interesting. Eventually, you have to make decisions, solve problems, and bring it to a point where someone else can actually use it.

That is why I have started valuing finished projects more.

They are imperfect records of what I was able to learn and build at that point in time.

And the next project can always be better.

title: AI Can Write Code, But It Cannot Build Your Experience
excerpt: AI has changed the way I build. I can ask questions faster. I can understand unfamiliar code more easily. I can generate a starting point for an idea that might have...
body:
AI has changed the way I build.

I can ask questions faster. I can understand unfamiliar code more easily. I can generate a starting point for an idea that might have taken much longer before.

That is useful.

But I think there is an important difference between using AI to help you build and using AI to avoid learning how things work.

AI Can Give You an Answer

AI can generate code for a feature in seconds.

It can explain an error. It can suggest a database structure. It can help you understand a framework you have never used before.

The speed is impressive.

But receiving an answer is not always the same as understanding it.

If the generated code breaks, you still need to know how to investigate the problem.

If a feature does not work as expected, you need to understand what part of the system is responsible.

Otherwise, you can end up with an application that works until something changes.

Then you are left staring at code that you technically own but do not fully understand.

The Goal Should Be Understanding

I do not think developers should avoid AI.

That would be like refusing to use search engines because books already exist.

Tools change.

The important question is how we use them.

For me, AI is most useful when it helps me understand something faster.

I might ask it to explain a concept. I might ask why an error is happening. I might use generated code as a starting point and then study how it works.

Sometimes the AI solution is wrong.

That is useful too.

Finding out why something is wrong forces you to understand the problem instead of blindly accepting the first answer.

Your Experience Cannot Be Generated

AI can generate code.

It cannot experience the hours you spent debugging a project. It cannot replace the decisions you made while designing something. It cannot give you the confidence that comes from solving a problem yourself.

Those experiences slowly become part of how you think as a developer.

Over time, you start recognizing patterns.

You become better at asking questions.

You become less afraid of unfamiliar problems because you have solved difficult ones before.

That is something no generated response can hand to you.

AI can make the journey faster.

But you still have to take the journey.

title: Why I'm Building Before I Feel Ready
excerpt: There are still many things I do not know. Sometimes I look at projects made by experienced developers and immediately see how far I still have to go.
body:
There are still many things I do not know.

Sometimes I look at projects made by experienced developers and immediately see how far I still have to go.

There are technologies I have not learned yet. Concepts I still struggle to understand. Problems that I would not know how to solve without searching for help.

For a long time, that felt like a reason to wait.

I thought I needed to learn more before building something serious.

I no longer think that is true.

You Can Always Learn One More Thing

Technology has a strange way of making you feel behind.

There is always another framework. Another programming language. Another AI tool. Another database. Another course.

You can spend years preparing to build something.

At some point, you have to start anyway.

You do not need to know everything to build the first version of an idea.

You only need to know enough to begin.

The rest can be learned while you are building.

Building Shows You What You Actually Need to Learn

When I study without building anything, it can sometimes be difficult to know what knowledge is actually important.

A project changes that.

Suddenly, you have a real reason to learn something.

You need authentication because your application has users. You need a database because your application needs to store information. You need to understand APIs because your frontend needs to communicate with something else.

The project creates the questions.

Then you learn because you need answers.

That process feels more practical to me.

Instead of trying to learn everything before starting, I can learn the things the project requires as I continue building.

Being Ready Is Not Always the Starting Point

I think many beginners wait because they are afraid of building something imperfect.

The first version might have bad code.

The design might change.

The project might fail.

All of that is possible.

But waiting does not remove those possibilities.

The only difference is that you have not learned anything from them yet.

Every project I build will probably show me something I could have done better.

I am starting to see that as part of the process.

The goal is not to create a perfect project on the first attempt.

The goal is to build something, learn from the problems, and carry those lessons into the next thing.

So I'm Building Anyway

I am still learning.

I still search for answers. I still make mistakes. I still encounter code that makes absolutely no sense to me for a few minutes, or sometimes a few hours.

But I would rather learn while building than wait until I feel completely ready.

Because I am starting to think that feeling completely ready may never arrive.

There will always be another thing to learn.

So for now, I am building with what I know.

And learning the rest along the way.
